label: Pre-1946 · Wartime & older
summary: Solid brick or balloon-frame construction, usually with empty wall cavities, minimal original attic insulation, and lots of air leakage. These homes have the biggest savings potential in Ontario — and a few safety flags worth knowing before you insulate.

typical.walls: Often little or no insulation (solid masonry or empty stud cavities)
typical.attic: Minimal unless topped up by a previous owner
typical.airtightness: Very leaky — often 2–4× a modern home
typical.windows: Original single-pane (sometimes with storms) unless replaced
typical.basement: Stone or early concrete foundation, almost never insulated

watchFor.detail: Common before ~1950. Insulation can't be blown over live knob-and-tube — electricians and ESA rules come first, and insurers care. Budget for an electrical check before insulating walls or attic.
Loose grey-brown pebbly insulation may contain asbestos (Zonolite era). Don't disturb it — testing and, if needed, professional removal come before any attic work.
Classic symptoms of attic bypasses — warm air leaking into the attic and melting roof snow.

priorities.why: The cheapest big win in a leaky home — attic hatches, top plates, rim joists, chases.

priorities.action: Attic to R-60 (after sealing & safety checks)
priorities.why: Highest return per dollar once bypasses are sealed.
Uninsulated foundations can lose 20%+ of a home's heat.
Drill-and-fill for frame walls; interior/exterior strategies for solid brick — get advice before committing.

priorities.action: Right-sized heat pump at equipment end-of-life
priorities.why: After envelope work, a smaller, cheaper unit heats the whole house properly.

auditAngle: An EnerGuide blower door test usually reads very high here, and the thermal camera finds empty wall sections and attic bypasses you can't see. The audit also documents pre-retrofit condition — required for the HRSP assessment-path rebates.

label: 1946–1965 · Post-war
summary: Post-war bungalows, storeys-and-a-half, and early splits. Walls have a little insulation (R-7 or so if any), attics are thin, basements bare, and many still run original or second-generation heating. Attic top-ups and basement insulation are the classic wins.

typical.walls: 2×4 frame with thin batts or none (~R-0 to R-7)
typical.attic: R-10 to R-20 — well below today's R-60 target
typical.airtightness: Leaky, especially at rim joists and attic penetrations
typical.windows: Single or early double-pane unless replaced
typical.basement: Unfinished, uninsulated concrete is the norm

watchFor.detail: This era is squarely in the vermiculite window — check before disturbing attic insulation.
Homes at the tail end of this era may have aluminum branch wiring — an electrician should verify connections before renovations.
Former oil homes may have buried or basement tank remnants; insurers and lenders ask.

priorities.why: Cheap, fast, and usually the single best payback in this era.

priorities.action: Air sealing with the attic work
priorities.why: Sealing before insulating locks in the gain.
Large bare-concrete heat loss; also makes basements usable.

priorities.action: Heat pump (or hybrid) at furnace end-of-life
priorities.why: These homes often have ductwork already — a straightforward swap.
Comfort and noise improve more than bills — do envelope first.

auditAngle: The audit quantifies exactly how thin the attic and basement are and models which order of upgrades hits the HRSP two-upgrade minimum for the $600 assessment rebate plus insulation rebates.

label: 1966–1980 · Suburban expansion
summary: Side-splits, back-splits, and early subdivisions. Some wall insulation (R-8 to R-12), modest attics, lots of electric baseboard from the 1970s — which makes this era Ontario's best heat-pump hunting ground.

typical.windows: Double-pane aluminum or early vinyl unless replaced
typical.basement: Partially finished, often uninsulated behind the finish

watchFor.detail: Common in 1970s builds. Swapping to a cold-climate heat pump typically cuts heating electricity 40–60% — and HRSP pays up to $12,000 for it.
Verify with an electrician before renovation work.
Urea-formaldehyde foam was used briefly; it mostly matters for disclosure, but know if you have it.

priorities.why: The biggest bill cut available to electrically heated homes of this era.
Still thin by modern standards; cheap win.
Split-levels leak at the many wall-roof junctions.

priorities.action: Insulate behind basement finishes when renovating
priorities.why: Catch it during any basement project.
Low-cost trim on any heating system.

auditAngle: For baseboard-heated homes, the audit's heat-loss calculation right-sizes the heat pump — the difference between a unit that keeps up at -20°C and one that doesn't.

label: 1981–1995 · Poly & batts
summary: Tighter construction with poly vapour barriers, R-12 to R-20 walls, and R-32-ish attics — but usually no heat-recovery ventilation, so humidity and stale air show up. Mid-efficiency furnaces from this era are overdue for replacement.

typical.windows: Double-pane; early low-E toward the end
typical.basement: Sometimes insulated to code minimums of the day

watchFor.detail: Tight-ish envelope without an HRV — window condensation and musty air are ventilation problems, not window problems.
If the furnace predates ~2000 it's burning 20%+ more gas than needed — decision point for heat pump vs. high-efficiency gas.

priorities.action: Heat pump or hybrid at furnace replacement
priorities.why: The natural upgrade moment for this era's aging equipment.

priorities.action: Add an HRV if humidity is an issue
priorities.why: Fixes condensation at the source.
Modest but cheap.
Rim joists and attic penetrations still leak.

priorities.action: Heat pump water heater at tank end-of-life
priorities.why: HRSP pays $500 toward it.

auditAngle: The audit separates ventilation problems from insulation problems — the two get confused constantly in this era, and the wrong diagnosis wastes thousands on windows.

label: 1996–2010 · Code era
summary: Reasonably insulated (R-40 attics late in the era), double-glazed, mostly high- or mid-efficiency gas. The wins are targeted: attic top-ups, duct sealing, equipment swaps at end-of-life, and fixing the bonus-room-over-garage cold spot.

watchFor.detail: The classic cold room — floor insulation gaps and duct runs through unconditioned space.
Leaky, unbalanced ducts make second floors hot in summer and cold in winter.

priorities.why: Still worthwhile at today's prices.

priorities.action: Heat pump / hybrid at AC or furnace replacement
priorities.why: Replace the AC with a heat pump and get heating included.
Comfort fix for uneven rooms.
Cheap trim.
HRSP offers up to $10,000; newer roofs make better hosts.

auditAngle: Diagnostics matter more than insulation depth here — duct testing and the thermal camera find the specific comfort failures worth fixing.

label: 2011+ · Modern code
summary: Close to current code: decent envelope, HRV likely, high-efficiency gas or electric. Audits here are about optimization and planning — heat pump timing, solar sizing, EV load planning — plus fixing any builder shortcuts.

watchFor.detail: Missed insulation bays and unbalanced HVAC show up even in new homes — and warranty windows are finite.
Builder-spec furnaces and ACs are routinely oversized, cycling hard and wearing early.

priorities.why: Up to $10,000 under HRSP; newer roofs and panels pair well.

priorities.action: Heat pump at first equipment replacement
priorities.why: Lock in the swap when the AC dies rather than buying AC-only again.
Cheap optimization for tight homes.
A blower door test confirms the builder delivered what code promised.

auditAngle: Use the audit as a commissioning check — verify the envelope you paid for, and get the EnerGuide label that helps at resale.
